sections.heading: The making — facts the examiner starts with

blocks.text: The Constitution was framed by the **Constituent Assembly**, set up under the **Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946**. It took **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**, was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (celebrated as **Constitution Day / Samvidhan Divas**) and came fully into force on **26 January 1950** — the date chosen to honour the **Purna Swaraj** resolution of 1930. **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting Committee**; **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** presided over the Assembly. The **Objectives Resolution**, moved by **Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946** and adopted on **22 January 1947**, became the philosophical soul of the Preamble.

items: Originally: **395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules**. Today (after ~106 amendments): about **470 Articles, 25 Parts, 12 Schedules** — the **lengthiest written constitution** of any sovereign state.

Reasons for length: geographical vastness and diversity, a **single constitution for Union and States**, the heavy imprint of the **Government of India Act, 1935**, and inclusion of administrative detail to avoid ambiguity.

rows: Single document for Union + States, detailed administration
Some provisions by special majority, some by simple majority, some need state ratification
Executive responsible to legislature; nominal vs real executive
Single hierarchy with Supreme Court at apex, enforces Union and state laws
Non-justiciable goals of a welfare state
Added by **42nd Amendment, 1976** on **Swaran Singh Committee** advice
No state religion; equal respect to all — 'principled distance'
Every citizen 18+ votes (61st Amendment reduced from 21)
Only Indian citizenship, unlike the USA
Converts federal structure into unitary during crises
Federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions, administrative detail (the largest single source)
Parliamentary system, rule of law, legislative procedure, single citizenship, cabinet system, prerogative writs, bicameralism
Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, impeachment of President, removal of judges, post of Vice-President
Directive Principles, nomination of members to Rajya Sabha, method of electing the President
Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, Centre-appointed Governors, advisory jurisdiction of Supreme Court
Concurrent List, freedom of inter-state trade (**Art 301**), joint sitting of the two Houses
Fundamental Duties, ideals of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble
Republic; ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity
Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency
Procedure for amendment, election of Rajya Sabha members

blocks.text: The 'bag of borrowings' jibe misses the point: the framers practised **creative adaptation, not imitation** — every borrowed device was modified to Indian conditions (e.g. the American 'due process' was deliberately replaced by the Japanese 'procedure established by law' to balance liberty with social reform).

sections.heading: The Preamble — identity card of the Constitution

blocks.text: The Preamble declares India a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic** securing **Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity**. The words **'Socialist', 'Secular'** and **'Integrity'** were inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** — the only amendment of the Preamble so far. Judicial journey: **Berubari Union case (1960)** — Preamble is *not* part of the Constitution; **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — reversed, Preamble *is* part of the Constitution and embodies the **basic structure**; **LIC of India (1995)** — reaffirmed, though it is non-justiciable and confers no power.

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Indian Constitution] --> B[Part III: Fundamental Rights - justiciable]
  A --> C[Part IV: Directive Principles - non-justiciable]
  A --> D[Part IVA: Fundamental Duties - 11 duties]
  B --> E[Courts enforce via Art 32 and Art 226]
  C --> F[Guide state policy - welfare state]
  D --> G[Moral obligations of citizens]
  E --> H[Balance: Minerva Mills 1980 - harmony between FRs and DPSPs is basic structure]
  F --> H

items: **Article 371D** (inserted by the **32nd Amendment, 1973**, after the Jai Andhra/Telangana agitations) empowers the President to provide **equitable opportunities in public employment and education** across regions of AP — basis of the **Presidential Order (1975)**, local cadres, and the **AP Administrative Tribunal**. It continues to apply to both AP and Telangana after 2014.
The **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** — enacted under **Articles 3 and 4** by simple majority — is the living proof that India is 'an **indestructible Union of destructible states**'.
**Fifth Schedule** applies to the Scheduled Areas of AP (agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam, Eluru, ASR district etc.), giving the Governor special report duties.

blocks.text: Exam tip: For any 'salient features' question, structure the answer as written-ness → blend of rigidity/flexibility → parliamentary → federal-with-unitary-bias → rights/duties/DPSP trinity → independent judiciary, and close with Granville Austin's phrase that the Constitution is 'first and foremost a social document'.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — the amendment-power saga & basic structure

blocks.text: The single most tested theme is the **evolution of Parliament's amending power under Article 368** — a duel between parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy. Trace it as a chain and you can answer almost any 'basic structure' question.

rows: Parliament can amend even Fundamental Rights; 'law' in Art 13 means ordinary law, not a constitutional amendment (1st Amendment upheld).
Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad; but Justice Hidayatullah first doubted whether FRs are 'a plaything' of majorities.
Reversed: Parliament CANNOT abridge Fundamental Rights; an amendment IS 'law' under Art 13. Prospective overruling used.
Landmark (13-judge bench, 7:6): Parliament can amend any part INCLUDING FRs, but cannot alter the **basic structure**. Overruled Golak Nath; upheld 24th Amendment.
Struck down the 39th Amendment clause shielding the PM's election — free & fair elections held to be basic structure.
Struck down 42nd Amendment parts: limited amending power & judicial review are basic structure; harmony between FRs and DPSPs is basic structure.
Basic-structure test applies to amendments made AFTER 24 April 1973 (the Kesavananda date); Ninth Schedule entries added later are testable.
Laws in the **Ninth Schedule** post-1973 are open to basic-structure review — no blanket immunity (Art 31B).

blocks.text: **Recent constitutional milestones every APPSC aspirant must cite (2019–2025):** the **abrogation of Article 370** (upheld in *In re: Article 370*, Dec 2023); the **Electoral Bonds scheme struck down** as unconstitutional (*ADR v. Union*, Feb 2024) for violating the voter's right to information under Art 19(1)(a); the **sub-classification of Scheduled Castes** permitted (*Davinder Singh*, 7-judge bench, Aug 2024) overruling *E.V. Chinnaiah*; and the **103rd Amendment (EWS reservation)** upheld in *Janhit Abhiyan* (2022). These show the basic-structure and equality doctrines as living law.

**Philosophical anchors for a top-scoring answer:** Granville Austin called the Constitution a **'seamless web'** and 'the cornerstone of a nation'; Ambedkar defended it as workable, flexible and strong; Nani Palkhivala termed the basic-structure doctrine 'the greatest contribution of the Indian judiciary to constitutional jurisprudence'. Close with the idea of **constitutional morality** (invoked in *Navtej Johar*, *Sabarimala*) — fidelity to constitutional values over majoritarian sentiment.

prelimsPointers: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — 13-judge bench (largest ever), verdict 7:6, propounded the **basic structure doctrine**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** — struck down Sections 4 & 55 of the 42nd Amendment; judicial review & limited amending power are basic structure.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)** — Ninth Schedule laws added after 24 April 1973 are subject to basic-structure review.
**Article 370** abrogated on 5 August 2019; Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in December 2023.
**Electoral Bonds Scheme** declared unconstitutional in February 2024 (ADR v. Union of India).
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** — anti-defection (Tenth Schedule); **Speaker's decision** subject to judicial review.

glossary.definition: Adherence to the core principles and spirit of the Constitution (liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity) even against prevailing social or majoritarian sentiment; invoked in Navtej Johar (2018) and Indian Young Lawyers Association / Sabarimala (2018).
Doctrine (first used in Golak Nath, 1967) by which a court's new interpretation applies only to future cases, leaving past transactions undisturbed.

prelimsPointers: Constituent Assembly first met **9 December 1946**; Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was interim President, **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** permanent President.
**Objectives Resolution**: moved 13 Dec 1946 by Nehru, adopted 22 Jan 1947.
Drafting Committee (29 Aug 1947) had **7 members**, chaired by **B.R. Ambedkar**.
Adopted **26 Nov 1949**; Articles 5, 6, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379 etc. came into force immediately; the rest on **26 Jan 1950**.
Preamble amended only once — **42nd Amendment 1976** (Socialist, Secular, Integrity).
**Article 371D** is AP-specific (extended to Telangana by the 2014 Act); inserted by the **32nd Amendment, 1973**.
National emblem's motto **'Satyameva Jayate'** is from the **Mundaka Upanishad**; the design was adopted on 26 January 1950.
mainsAngles: 'The Indian Constitution is a bag of borrowings' — critically examine (line: borrowed forms, indigenous spirit; creative adaptation).
Discuss how the Constitution blends rigidity with flexibility, with reference to Article 368 and judicial review of amendments.
'Federal in form, unitary in spirit' — evaluate this description of the Indian Constitution (Wheare vs Austin vs Bommai).
Examine the continuing relevance of Article 371D for Andhra Pradesh after the 2014 bifurcation.
Granville Austin called the Constitution 'a social document' — substantiate with reference to Parts III and IV.

glossary.definition: The introductory statement of the Constitution declaring its source (We, the People), the nature of the polity (Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic) and its objectives (Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity); part of the Constitution per Kesavananda Bharati (1973) but non-justiciable.

Doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) that Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368 but cannot destroy its basic features (e.g., supremacy of the Constitution, secularism, judicial review, federalism).

Article 21 standard (borrowed from Japan) under which the State may deprive a person of life or liberty by a validly enacted procedure; after Maneka Gandhi (1978) the procedure must also be just, fair and reasonable — importing due-process content.
K.C. Wheare's description of India: a system federal in form but with pronounced unitary features such as emergency powers, single citizenship, All-India Services and a strong Centre.

Special provision (32nd Amendment, 1973) empowering the President to secure equitable opportunities in public employment and education for people of different regions of Andhra Pradesh; basis of local cadres and the AP Administrative Tribunal.
Constitution Day, celebrated on 26 November every year (since 2015) marking the adoption of the Constitution in 1949.

sections.heading: The constitutional design of two governments

blocks.text: India has a **dual polity**: the **Union government** (Part V) and **State governments** (Part VI), each with its own executive, legislature and defined field of action. The field is demarcated by the **Seventh Schedule** read with **Articles 245–246** (territorial and subject-matter distribution) and by **Articles 73 and 162**, which make the **executive power co-extensive with legislative power** at each level.

rows: **President (Arts 52–62)** — nominal head; acts on aid & advice (**Art 74**)
**PM + Council of Ministers (Art 75)**, collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (**75(3)**)
**CM + Council of Ministers (Art 164)**, responsible to Assembly (**164(2)**)
**Art 73** — matters on which Parliament can legislate
**Art 162** — matters on which the State legislature can legislate
Legislature (**Art 168**): Governor + Assembly (+ Council in AP — bicameral)

sections.heading: Who does what — the Seventh Schedule

rows: Defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, currency, railways, banking, communications, census, citizenship
Local/regional importance; State legislates (Parliament can intrude via **Arts 249, 250, 252, 253, 356**)
Public order, **police**, public health, agriculture, land, prisons, local government, markets
Both; Union law prevails on repugnancy (**Art 254**)
Criminal law & procedure, marriage, education, forests, trade unions, electricity, population control

items: **Residuary power** is with the Union (**Art 248; Entry 97 List I**) — the Canadian model.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** shifted five subjects to the Concurrent List: **education, forests, weights & measures, protection of wild animals & birds, administration of justice**.
In a conflict, **predominance runs Union List → Concurrent List → State List**.

sections.heading: Duties of the Union towards the States

items: **Art 355** — duty of the Union to **protect states** against external aggression and internal disturbance, and to ensure state government is carried on per the Constitution.
**Arts 256–257** — states must comply with Union laws; the Union may give **directions**; failure can invite **Art 365 → Art 356** consequences.
**Art 275 & 280** — statutory grants and Finance Commission devolution: the fiscal duty of the Union to correct imbalance.
**Art 263** — Inter-State Council to coordinate; **Art 262** — adjudication of inter-state river water disputes.

  A --> C[State List 61 - State Legislature]
  A --> D[Concurrent List 52 - Both]
  D --> E[Repugnancy: Union law prevails - Art 254]
  C --> F[Exceptions: Arts 249 250 252 253 - Parliament enters State List]
  A --> G[Residuary: Art 248 with Union]

sections.heading: The AP dimension — a state built by these provisions

items: The **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** imposed specific **duties on the Union towards AP**: special assistance for **backward districts (Rayalaseema & north-coastal AP)**, declaring **Polavaram** a **national project**, tax incentives, and establishing Schedule-13 institutions (IIT Tirupati, IIM Visakhapatnam, NIT Tadepalligudem, IIIT, Central University of AP at Anantapur, AIIMS Mangalagiri, IISER Tirupati, etc.).
AP is one of the six states with a **Legislative Council (Art 169)** — revived in 2007, giving it a bicameral legislature.

Everyday governance in AP illustrates the lists: **police and land** (State List) run village/ward secretariats and revenue administration, while **railways, ports (major), telecom** (Union List) shape Visakhapatnam's economy.

blocks.text: Exam tip: When asked about 'functions and duties' of governments, do NOT just reproduce the lists — organise the answer as (1) constitutional demarcation, (2) executive co-extensiveness (Arts 73/162), (3) the Union's protective and fiscal duties towards states, and (4) one live illustration (AP Reorganisation Act obligations works perfectly).

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — doctrines that decide Centre–State legislative disputes

blocks.text: Distribution of powers is examined through the **interpretive doctrines** courts use when Union and State laws collide. Master these five and you can argue any legislative-competence question.

rows: If the true nature of a law falls within the legislature's list, incidental encroachment on another list is valid.
'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' — a legislature cannot disguise an ultra vires law.
On a Concurrent subject, Union law prevails over a conflicting State law unless the State law has Presidential assent.
A State law may operate on objects outside the State if there is a sufficient connection.
Overlapping entries are read so that each is given effect; no entry is rendered nugatory.

blocks.text: **Parliament can legislate on the State List in five constitutional situations** — a favourite one-mark and mains hook: (1) **Art 249** — Rajya Sabha resolution of national interest (2/3 majority); (2) **Art 250** — during a National Emergency; (3) **Art 252** — two or more States request it (e.g., the *Wildlife Act*, *Water Act*); (4) **Art 253** — to implement international treaties/agreements; (5) **Art 356** — during President's Rule.

**Recent flashpoints:** the **97th Amendment** (cooperative societies) was struck down by the SC in *Union of India v. Rajendra Shah* (2021) insofar as it touched cooperatives — a **State subject** — for want of state ratification, a vivid lesson on Art 368(2); the **three farm laws (2020)** provoked a federalism storm over 'agriculture' and 'markets' (State List) versus 'trade & commerce' (Union/Concurrent), and were repealed in 2021. Both illustrate that the **Seventh Schedule is politically live, not a dead letter.**

mainsAngles: Explain the doctrine of pith and substance and its role in resolving Centre–State legislative conflicts with case law.
'Article 252 is cooperative federalism in its purest form' — discuss with examples.

glossary.definition: Doctrine that judges a law by its true subject matter; if that lies within the enacting legislature's competence, incidental trespass on another list does not invalidate it.
A law that pretends to act within power but in substance exceeds it; void on the maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.

prelimsPointers: Executive power of the Union is vested in the **President (Art 53)**; of the state in the **Governor (Art 154)**.
Council of Ministers headed by PM must **aid and advise** the President — advice binding after the **42nd/44th Amendments** (Art 74).
Union List **100 entries**, State List **61**, Concurrent List **52** (post-42nd Amendment shifts).
**Residuary powers**: Art 248 read with **Entry 97, Union List**.
Ministry size capped at **15% of the lower House** by the **91st Amendment, 2003**.
**Art 355** — Union's duty to protect states; **Art 365** — consequence of not complying with Union directions.
**Polavaram** was declared a national project under the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014**.
mainsAngles: Discuss the scheme of distribution of executive powers between the Union and the States, and how Articles 256–257 tilt it towards the Centre.
'The Union's duty under Article 355 is both a shield and a sword' — critically examine with reference to its use to justify Article 356.
Examine whether the 42nd Amendment's transfer of education and forests to the Concurrent List strengthened governance or weakened federalism.
Evaluate the Union government's discharge of its statutory obligations to Andhra Pradesh under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.

glossary.definition: Constitutional arrangement of two levels of government — Union and State — each deriving authority directly from the Constitution and acting within its own demarcated sphere.
Principle in Articles 73 and 162 that a government's executive power extends to all matters on which its legislature can make laws.
Conflict between a Union and a State law on a Concurrent List subject; the Union law prevails, unless the State law received Presidential assent (and even then Parliament can override).
Power to legislate on matters not enumerated in any of the three lists; vested in Parliament under Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List.
Principle (Arts 75(3), 164(2)) that the Council of Ministers stands or falls together, answerable to the directly elected House.

blocks.text: The Constitution nowhere uses the word 'federation' — **Article 1** calls India a **'Union of States'**, signalling (per Ambedkar) that the federation is **not the result of an agreement** and that **no state may secede**. India displays all classical federal features — **dual polity, written constitution, division of powers, constitutional supremacy, rigidity, independent judiciary, bicameralism** — alongside pronounced **unitary features**.

rows: **Art 3**: Parliament alone alters state boundaries/names — 'indestructible Union of destructible states'
**Emergency provisions (Arts 352/356/360)** convert the polity into a unitary one
**Governor** as Centre's agent; reservation of bills (**Arts 200–201**)
Unequal Rajya Sabha representation; residuary powers with the Centre; **fiscal dependence of states**

blocks.text: Verdicts: **K.C. Wheare** — 'quasi-federal'; **Granville Austin** — '**cooperative federalism**'; **Ivor Jennings** — 'federation with a strong centralising tendency'; and the Supreme Court in **S.R. Bommai (1994)** — **federalism is part of the basic structure**.

items: **Office of the Governor** — partisan appointments, sitting on bills (Arts 200–201), discretion in hung assemblies. **Punchhi Commission (2010)** recommended a fixed 5-year term and removal only through impeachment-like process; **SC in State of Punjab v. Governor (2023)** held Governors cannot indefinitely withhold assent.
**Misuse of Article 356** — used over 130 times, curbed by **S.R. Bommai (1994)**: floor test is the venue for testing majority; proclamation is judicially reviewable.

**Fiscal federalism** — vertical imbalance (states incur ~60% of expenditure but raise ~40% of revenue); mounting **cesses and surcharges** (outside the divisible pool) shrink states' effective share below the **41% recommended by the 15th Finance Commission**.

**GST and lost autonomy** — states surrendered sales-tax powers to the **GST Council (Art 279A)**; the end of guaranteed compensation (2022) and the **Mohit Minerals (2022)** ruling (Council recommendations are not binding — 'cooperative federalism is a dialogue') keep this contested.
**Concurrent-List creep** — central laws on state-list-adjacent fields (e.g., the three farm laws, 2020–21, touching agricultural markets) provoke friction.

**Inter-state river water disputes (Art 262)** — the **Krishna (KWDT-I & II)** and **Godavari** tribunals are existential for AP; the **AP–Telangana** sharing dispute after 2014 remains unresolved; the Krishna River Management Board's jurisdiction was notified only in 2021.

**Institutional atrophy** — the **Inter-State Council (Art 263)**, created on Sarkaria's advice in 1990, meets rarely; **NITI Aayog** (2015) replaced Planning Commission transfers with a think-tank role, weakening a fiscal channel while promoting '**competitive federalism**' (rankings, Aspirational Districts).

**Special Category Status** — abolished as a general mechanism after the 14th Finance Commission; **AP's continuing demand for SCS**, promised on the floor of the Rajya Sabha in 2014, is the sharpest current illustration of trust deficit in Union–state relations.

  A --> C[Fiscal: cesses, GST, FC devolution]

rows: Art 356 as a **last resort**; consultation with CM before appointing Governor; permanent Inter-State Council (created 1990)
Fixed tenure for Governors; 'localised emergency'; Governor's discretion narrowed; National Integration Council reforms

blocks.text: Way forward: institutionalise the **Inter-State Council** as the apex dialogue forum, widen the **divisible pool** to include cesses, time-bound gubernatorial assent, respect the **Bommai** discipline, and treat the GST Council's dialogic model — 'cooperative federalism as a **dialogue**' (Mohit Minerals) — as the template. Federalism, as Austin said, must remain **cooperative in structure and bargaining in spirit**.

Exam tip: An APPSC answer on federal challenges that cites the AP-specific wounds — Special Category Status, Krishna water sharing, pending Reorganisation Act promises — alongside Bommai and the Finance Commission will always outscore a generic all-India answer.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — federalism in 2023–2026: verdicts, fiscal frontier & AP

blocks.text: Federalism is the most dynamic Paper-III theme; examiners reward the **latest developments**. Anchor your answer in these.

items: **Governor's assent settled (2023–24):** in *State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor* (2023) and *State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor* (April 2025), the SC held Governors cannot pocket-veto bills; the Tamil Nadu verdict for the first time invoked **Article 142 to declare ten bills 'deemed assented'** and read timelines into Arts 200–201 — a landmark curbing gubernatorial obstruction.

**Delimitation & the southern anxiety (2026 horizon):** the freeze on Lok Sabha seat re-allocation ends after the first census post-2026; southern states (including AP) fear losing parliamentary weight for having controlled population — a fresh federal fault-line linking demography, representation and fiscal share.

**Fiscal federalism forward:** the **16th Finance Commission** (chair **Arvind Panagariya**, award period 2026–31) is examining vertical devolution, the swelling share of **cesses & surcharges** outside the divisible pool, and the treatment of GST; the **GST compensation cess** was extended past 2022 only to repay borrowings, sharpening states' revenue anxiety.

**Money-and-mandate tools:** central control via **All-India Services (Art 312)**, centrally sponsored schemes with rigid conditionalities, and the shift from Planning Commission grants to **NITI Aayog**'s advisory role continue to tilt the balance centreward while promoting 'competitive federalism'.

blocks.text: **The Andhra Pradesh federal ledger (use these to localise every answer):** the unfulfilled promise of **Special Category Status** (assured on the floor of the Rajya Sabha in 2014); the **Krishna water-sharing dispute** with Telangana and the delayed operationalisation of the **Krishna River Management Board**; pending **Polavaram** funding as a national project; and Schedule-13 institutional commitments under the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014**. These are the sharpest live illustrations of the Union–State trust deficit.
